Web design Louisville owners can live with has to handle one thing most cities never think about: a calendar that rewrites your week every spring. For about two weeks before the first Saturday in May, the Kentucky Derby Festival fills the riverfront and the streets, downtown hotels fill up and visitors look up places to eat, drink and get their car fixed on a phone. Then it ends, and the regulars come back. A website that cannot change as fast as the town does starts telling customers the wrong thing.

Dominion Web Design Pro is Maurice Johnson, a one-person web design business in East Texas. He writes each page by hand, shows you a free demo of your site before you pay, and prints his prices: $497, $997 or $1,997, one time. This page explains how we would plan a site for a Louisville business, and what we leave to others.

Louisville web design that expects the spring rush

The 2026 Kentucky Derby Festival opened with Thunder Over Louisville on Saturday, April 18, and ran more than seventy events before Derby 152 on May 2: a waterfront festival, a balloon race, the miniMarathon and marathon, the Pegasus Parade, the Great Steamboat Race and more. Tourism officials put the 2023 Derby's economic impact above $401 million, with downtown hotels close to 98% full.

That money reaches far past Churchill Downs. It lands at the barber who opens early on Oaks day, the caterer booked for a dozen Derby parties, the cleaner turning over short-term rentals between guests, and the HVAC tech whose phone rings when a rental's air quits with a full house. Each of them needs the website to say something different in late April than it said in February.

For a turnover cleaner, that might be a booking page that opens extra slots for race weekend and closes them the following Monday. For a restaurant, it is a notice with festival hours and whether you take reservations. For a contractor, it might be nothing more than a line that says you are still answering calls that week.

None of this needs a complicated system. It needs a site built with room for a seasonal notice, and someone who will post it when you ask.

A Louisville year, and what your site should say in each part

Here is a simple plan for keeping pages honest through the seasons. Use the parts that fit your business.

Time of yearWhat is happeningWhat to change on the site
Late winterVisitors start booking for springPost event packages, catering dates or rental availability early, while people are planning
Mid AprilThunder Over Louisville opens the FestivalAdd a short notice with special hours, parking tips and how to reach you
Late April to the first Saturday in MayFestival events, then Oaks and DerbyKeep the booking page current daily; take sold-out dates off so nobody calls for them
The week after DerbyVisitors leave, regulars returnPull the event notices and put your everyday offer back up front
Summer and fallBourbon visitors, conventions, school startsRefresh photos and seasonal services, and check that hours match your Google profile

Whiskey Row and the businesses that live off bourbon visitors

Before Prohibition, a stretch of Main Street downtown held dozens of distillers, wholesalers and other spirits businesses, the heart of Kentucky's whiskey trade. The name Whiskey Row stuck. The revival is recent: the Evan Williams Bourbon Experience opened on West Main in 2013, and distilleries and tasting rooms have filled in around it. The city's Urban Bourbon Trail, started in 2008, steers visitors to bourbon bars and restaurants across town.

Most of the people who benefit do not make whiskey. They run the tour van, the boutique a block away, the photographer hired for a bachelorette weekend, the restaurant whose bourbon list is the reason a visitor walks in. A visitor deciding where to go next is standing on a sidewalk with a phone, so the page needs your address, hours, a tap-to-call number and a few honest photos near the top, not a slideshow that takes ten seconds to load.

Louisville website design starts with the names customers use

Ask someone where they live and you rarely hear "Louisville." You hear the Highlands, Germantown, Old Louisville, St. Matthews, Jeffersontown, the West End. Google says it ranks local results on relevance, distance and prominence, and a page that plainly names the area you serve gives it something relevant to match.

  • NuLuThe East Market District, known for galleries, antique and specialty shops and restaurants that lean on local farms. Shops here sell as much to visitors as to neighbors.
  • The HighlandsBardstown Road runs through it, with a long commercial stretch of restaurants, bars and owner-run shops that locals call Restaurant Row.
  • Germantown and ButchertownOld neighborhoods just east of downtown. Butchertown was the city's meatpacking hub in the 1800s and now mixes old industry with new bars, a brandy distillery and the soccer stadium.
  • Across the OhioJeffersonville, Clarksville and New Albany sit on the Indiana bank. One Southern Indiana serves as the chamber for Clark and Floyd counties there.

For a plumber who works from Okolona to Prospect, or a dog groomer who draws from both sides of the river, this is where city pages earn their keep. The Pro package includes ten of them, each researched and written about that place instead of copied with a new name.

Web design in Louisville, KY that you do not have to maintain yourself

A common story goes like this: a nephew or a builder plan made the site, it went live, and nobody has touched it since. The hours are from 2022 and the specials are from a Derby three years gone. A seasonal town punishes that more than most, because the stale page is the one visitors see.

Our answer is simple. While you are on our hosting, maintenance and updates plan, you send a change and it gets made. That plan is $49 a month, or included while you keep the AI agent. An appointment business, such as a chiropractor or a salon, can move its booking hours for festival week with one email.

If you would rather edit pages yourself, a builder plan may suit you better, and we will say so. Plenty of good Louisville web design firms also offer training and editing access. What matters is deciding up front who updates the site, so it does not drift out of date by next spring.

Louisville help worth a call before you hire anyone

Kentucky SBDC, Louisville office

Part of the statewide Small Business Development Center network hosted by the University of Kentucky. The Louisville office has been in the network since 1982 and offers no-cost one-on-one counseling on business plans, financing, market research and getting started.

SCORE Kentucky

Volunteer mentors from an office on West Main Street downtown, covering Louisville, Lexington and Southern Indiana. Mentoring is free for the life of the business, in person, by email or by video.

One Louisville

Greater Louisville Inc., the metro chamber, merged with the Louisville Economic Development Alliance; the combined group took the name One Louisville on March 1, 2026, and now runs the chamber's member services and advocacy alongside economic development.

METCO loans from Louisville Metro

The Metropolitan Business Development Corporation, run through the city's Department of Economic Development, makes small business loans, including facade and accessibility loans for storefronts.

Common questions

What are typical web design rates in Louisville?

Rates vary from one designer to the next, and many firms quote only after a discovery call or bill by the hour. Ours are printed and paid once: $497 for the 5-page Starter, $997 for Pro and $1,997 for Agency. After launch, hosting, maintenance and updates are $49 a month, or included while you keep the AI agent. Ask anyone you compare whether small seasonal edits, like Derby week hours, are part of the monthly fee or billed separately.

Can my website switch to Derby week hours and then switch back?

Yes. A short notice bar or an events page can go up before Thunder Over Louisville and come down after the race, without touching the rest of the site. On our hosting plan you send the change by email or phone and it is made for you, so you are not logging in to a builder at midnight during the busiest week of your year.

Do you do ecommerce web design in Louisville?

For a small catalog, yes: a page of products with photos, prices and a way to order or ask, or links out to a checkout you already use. If you need a full online store with a large catalog, inventory sync and shipping rules, a dedicated ecommerce developer is the better hire, and we will tell you that before you spend anything.

Is Dominion Web Design Pro a Black-owned web design company?

Yes. Dominion Web Design Pro is owned by Maurice Johnson, a Black business owner, and he writes and builds each site himself. We do not claim any minority-business certification. We are in Big Sandy, Texas, not Louisville, and every project is handled by phone, email and shared links.

Should a Louisville business add pages for Jeffersonville or New Albany?

If you really take jobs or draw customers across the river, yes. People in Southern Indiana search by their own town names. A page written about the Indiana towns you serve, with honest details about how far you travel, does far more than a list of town names pasted at the bottom of the home page.
